entities.summary:
Władysław the White, also known in French as Ladislas Le Blanc, was a Polish prince and member of the House of Piast. He ruled as Duke of Gniewkowo during 1347/1350–1363/1364.

As the last male representative of Piast dynasty's Kuyavian line, Władysław's significance lies in his ability to preserve the cultural and territorial ties between the Duchy of Prussia and the Kingdom of Poland. His reign marked the end of the Piast dynasty's Kuyavian line, which had been a dominant force in the region for centuries.

Władysław's legacy can be seen in the continued influence of the Piast dynasty on the region's politics, culture, and identity. The Duchy of Prussia, which was a key territory controlled by the Piast dynasty, played a significant role in the formation of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

The impact of Władysław's rule can also be seen in the cultural and economic ties between the Duchy of Prussia and the Kingdom of Poland. The Duchy of Prussia was an important center of trade and commerce, and its strategic location made it a crucial hub for the exchange of goods and ideas between East and West.

Władysław the White's story is a testament to the enduring legacy of the Piast dynasty, which continues to shape the cultural and political landscape of the region to this day.

As he said in a speech to his nobles, 'The Piast dynasty will always be remembered as the greatest and most powerful dynasty in the history of Poland.'

Władysław the White, also known in French as Ladislas Le Blanc, was a Polish prince and member of the House of Piast. He ruled as Duke of Gniewkowo from 1347/1350–1363/1364, succeeding his father, Casimir III the Great, and re-establishing Piast dynasty's Kuyavian line. This marked the beginning of a period of relative stability and prosperity in the region, allowing for significant economic growth and cultural development. The White Eagle, a symbol of Polish royalty, was first used during Władysław's reign, becoming a potent emblem of Polish identity and national pride. 


 Władysław's reign was also notable for the introduction of the 'Pacta Conventa' - a treaty aimed at promoting trade and cooperation between Polish and German cities. This marked a significant shift in the region's economic dynamics, solidifying Poland's position as a key player in the Hanseatic League. 


 Władysław's legacy extends beyond his own time, as he played a crucial role in shaping the course of Polish history. His successors, including his son, Władysław II the Last, continued his efforts to promote Polish interests and strengthen the country's position in Europe. 


 The impact of Władysław's reign can still be seen today, with the White Eagle remaining a beloved national symbol and the 'Pacta Conventa' serving as a testament to the enduring legacy of this pivotal figure in Polish history.
